title: Shema Yisrael
hook: read the Shema's first two words in Hebrew

segments.voice: Yesterday, your first word: shalom, four letters and two marks. Your line was shalom, read. Who did you say it to? Today, two words, and they're the first two of the Shema. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

"Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Up to now on this path, you've met that line in English. In Deuteronomy, the verse after it says to speak these words when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise up. So it is said at bedtime and in the morning service, and tradition places it on the lips of children and of the dying. In the prayer book, it stands in Hebrew. And it opens with two words. Today those two words stop being sounds you've heard and become letters you can read. Shema Yisrael.
screen: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` → `LYING DOWN AND RISING UP.` → `TWO WORDS, IN HEBREW.`

segments.voice: Shema Yisrael. Read it four ways. First, shema. Three letters, right to left. Shin, with its dot on the right arm: sh. Under it, two dots stacked, a mark that here barely sounds at all. Then mem, with a short line under it: ma. Then ayin, the eye, which says nothing. Sh, ma, and silence. Shema. It means hear, or listen. Second, Yisrael. Start with yod, the small one, with a dot under it: yi. Then the letter with three arms again, but look: the dot has moved to the left arm. That makes it sin, and it says s. Yis. Then resh with the T-shaped mark under it: ra. Then alef, silent, carrying two dots side by side: eh. Then lamed. Yis, ra, el. Yisrael. Third, a detail in the scroll. By scribal tradition, in a Torah scroll the ayin at the end of shema and the dalet at the end of the verse's last word are written larger than the letters around them. Some readers notice that together they spell ed, a witness. That's a reading, not the verse's plain meaning, and it's offered as one. Fourth, a gesture. The Talmud tells of Rabbi Judah the Prince passing his hand over his eyes as he said the Shema, and a custom grew from it: covering the eyes for the first line. The eyes close. The ears open. It begins with listening.
screen: `SHEMA: SH, MA, AND A SILENT EYE.` · `YISRAEL: THE DOT MOVES LEFT.` · `TWO LETTERS WRITTEN LARGE.` · `EYES COVERED, EARS OPEN.` · then, large: `שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read them yourself. Settle, and breathe. Look at the two words on the screen. Start at the right. Sh, ma. Shema. Then the next word: yis, ra, el. Yisrael. Read them once slowly. Then, if you like, cover your eyes with your hand, the way the custom does, and say the two words again from memory. Sit in the dark behind your hand for a breath or two, listening. If you pray, you can say the whole first line. The bell holds the time.
Shema Yisrael. Hear, O Israel: the opening two words of the Shema, read now in Hebrew, right to left. Today's word.
Your line: read it yourself. Tonight, before sleep, read or say the two words once, the way the verse sets them at lying down. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Jews who keep the daily prayers say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and again at bedtime, and a common custom is to cover the eyes with the right hand while saying the first line.
